themes.theme: Procurement law, routes and market engagement
themes.definition: The rules and routes through which a public body goes to market for AI, from statutory procurement law and central playbooks to early engagement with suppliers and the way requirements are framed.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 restates the statutory duty to comply with procurement legislation (the Public Contract Regulations 2015 and the Procurement Act 2023), says central departments and their arm's length bodies follow the DDaT Playbook on a 'comply or explain' basis, and names the commercial team as leading the procurement. UK136 adds fair-market rules for central government buyers: preliminary market engagement 'must' observe the principles of public procurement so that no supplier gains an advantage, requirements should not discriminate against SMEs, VCSEs or suppliers from trade-agreement countries, and the same data should go to all suppliers at the same time. UK136 also recommends engaging AI suppliers early in planning, using output-based requirements that let suppliers propose their own solution, and engaging users and stakeholders to set the areas on which bids are assessed. UK082, a set of recommendations whose acceptance is not recorded in the text, proposes a more active central role in shaping the market: two-way partnerships in which government meets vendors' product teams to 'shape development', multi-stage 'Competitive Flexible Procedures' with startups compensated for each round, and national tenders led by mission delivery boards. There is a tension between UK136's rule that no supplier gains a preferential advantage in pre-market engagement and UK082's proposal that government shape particular vendors' product development before procurement [inference].
themes.holders: 'You' (government departments and public sector organisations); all central government departments and their arm's length bodies; 'your commercial team'; central government departments and procurement teams (UK136); government, AI vendors and startups, and 'the mission delivery boards' (UK082).
themes.binding: Statutory where procurement law is restated ('you must ensure you comply with procurement legislation'); 'comply or explain' for the DDaT Playbook; UK136's 'must' on preliminary market engagement restates procurement principles; the rest is 'should', imperative or 'consider' in non-statutory guidance, and UK082's items are recommendations with acceptance not recorded. No passage states what happens if the requirement is not met.
themes.checks: n/a (UK136 asks buyers to set bid-assessment areas with users and stakeholders, but this is an evaluation of suppliers' bids, not a check on a tool or its outputs)

themes.theme: Allocating responsibilities, risks, liabilities and ownership with suppliers
themes.definition: Arrangements, usually contractual, that set out which party in the buyer-supplier chain is responsible and liable for what, including intellectual property, licensing and end-of-contract roles.
themes.what_is_set_out: Several documents ask the buying body to make sure suppliers understand and accept their responsibilities. UK099 puts this as 'must' (make sure the supplier understands their responsibilities, and, per the coder note, agree what risks they must manage and ask them to share how the system works), while UK174 uses 'should' and 'ensure' (vendors understand their responsibilities and liabilities, put mitigations in place and share information; all parties in the life cycle act lawfully) and recommends working with legal experts on IP, transparency levels, liability distribution and error procedures. UK010 (Ofgem) says risks 'should be appropriately allocated in contractual arrangements along the supply chain' with legal responsibility and liability clearly articulated, and UK268 expects documentation defining the roles of both auditee and external provider. UK136 adds who owns new intellectual property, open standards and royalty-free licensing to avoid lock-in, and defined end-of-contract roles for authority and supplier. UK139 addresses the case where legal responsibility cannot be assigned to a supply-chain actor inside a regulator's remit, telling regulators to encourage actors within the remit to govern who they outsource to; this treats contractual governance as a substitute where legal responsibility runs out [inference].
themes.holders: The buying body ('you', 'you (as buyer of a data-driven or AI system)'), working with legal experts; vendors and suppliers as counterparties; 'Stakeholders and supply chain parties' (UK010); 'The auditee; the external provider' (UK268); 'Contracting authority and supplier' (UK136); 'the AI actors within the remit', encouraged by regulators (UK139).
themes.binding: UK099 uses 'must' in non-statutory guidance; UK174, UK010, UK268 and UK136 use 'should', 'ensure', 'consider' or good-practice controls; UK139 is non-binding ('encourage'). No consequence is stated in any passage.

themes.theme: Contract terms that carry standards, testing, fairness and audit duties to suppliers
themes.definition: Requirements the buying body is told to write into tenders and contracts so that the public sector's own standards (testing, transparency, audit, fairness, equality, codes of practice, security) also bind the supplier.
themes.what_is_set_out: The shared idea is that the contract carries the public body's own obligations through to the supplier. UK174 asks that expectations of responsible use be the same for procured and in-house systems and lists 'Implement transparency and auditing requirements for suppliers' as a practical recommendation; UK099 asks for fairness and equality clauses; and UK216 (EHRC) recommends making compliance with the Public Sector Equality Duty, and supply of the information needed to monitor the AI once implemented, a contractual requirement. UK071 asks teams to put clear testing expectations into contracts and tender documents (the coder note adds non-functional requirements for explainability, fairness, robustness and security), and UK082 says contract terms should set standards such as quality and best practice such as performance evaluations. UK136 asks that existing codes of practice, guidance and regulations be carried into the contract 'where suitable', and UK010 asks that data ownership, privacy, confidentiality and cyber security be reflected in commercial arrangements and that developers have robust arrangements, including (per the note) auditable training and appropriate testing. No passage says what test, standard or performance level the contract should require.
themes.holders: The buying body ('you', 'your team', 'teams (projects involving procurement or external suppliers)'), with commercial colleagues; public bodies in England (UK216); 'supply chain managers' (UK010); government as customer (UK082); suppliers and AI developers as the parties bound.
themes.binding: Recommendations ('should', 'we recommend', imperatives, 'may include'); UK082's recommendation has no recorded acceptance. Where the PSED is written into a contract (UK216), the underlying duty is statutory, but the contract term itself is only recommended [inference]. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Contractual testing and performance evaluation: trigger: set at tender and contract stage, with UK216's monitoring information needed 'once it is implemented' (ongoing); compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated (UK071's note names explainability, fairness, robustness and security as requirement areas, UK082 names 'quality' and 'performance evaluations'); who: the supplier complies and supplies information, the buyer monitors [inference for UK216]; what happens with the result: not stated.

themes.theme: Service levels, support and incident handling in supplier arrangements
themes.definition: Provisions that keep the buying body able to handle incidents, errors, outages and failures in a system that depends on a supplier's infrastructure or model.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK268, written for auditors, is the main source: where systems are purchased or rely on external models, service level agreements should ensure continuous support and enough control of external infrastructure for incident management and failure analysis, cloud and external model suppliers should be checked against security standards, and lifecycle management should cover procurement and contract management. UK174 says contracts for technology services 'may need to' include procedures for system errors and outages that recognise the consequences of performance failures. UK266 asks audit and risk assurance committees whether there is active management of new risks from cloud and third-party providers, such as reduced control over data and supply-chain exposure. The emphasis is on retaining control and access when something goes wrong, not on the quality of the supplier's model in normal operation.
themes.holders: Mostly passive or 'not stated' in UK268 (nearest: the auditee organisation and the external provider); 'not stated (nearest: you as buyer, with your lawyers)' in UK174; the organisation, questioned by its audit and risk assurance committee (UK266).
themes.binding: Good-practice 'expected' or 'possible' controls in an audit guide; 'may need to' (UK174); a question (UK266). No consequence stated; UK268 names the risk of 'Insufficient support of or control over purchased or externally developed sy…' (truncated in the input).

themes.theme: Supplier selection criteria: sustainability, security and contract type
themes.definition: Criteria the buying body is asked to apply when choosing a supplier, model provider or type of contract, beyond price and function.
themes.what_is_set_out: Two kinds of criteria appear. Environmental: UK174 recommends evaluating the environmental credentials of model providers and partners (renewable energy, efficient infrastructure, low-carbon grids), and UK099 asks for sustainability to be a supplier-selection criterion, with questions on energy use and carbon footprint before engaging a service (per the note). Security: UK099 asks that third-party suppliers who store, collect or process data be vetted and comply with the project's security requirements, without saying who vets or whether a supplier can be refused. AI_Insights, on AI coding assistants, strongly recommends using only business or enterprise contracts or locally run open-source models, because (per the note) free or personal-licence tools record prompts and responses to train the provider's models, and treats the added risk of a trusted provider that stores private code as acceptable under a business contract. Here the type of contract, rather than any test of the tool, is the safeguard.
themes.holders: 'You' as buyer (UK174, UK099); 'you (developers in HMG)' and the trusted provider (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: Recommendations, at most 'strongly recommended' (AI_Insights); AI_Insights' view that a trusted provider's added risk 'should be acceptable' under a business contract is a non-binding interpretation. No consequence stated.

themes.theme: Information requested from suppliers before purchase
themes.definition: Information the buying body is told to obtain from suppliers or developers during tendering or due diligence about how an AI system was built and how well it performs.
themes.what_is_set_out: This is where the cell is most specific about the performance of AI outputs. UK099 lists questions to consider asking a supplier before entering a contract, including (per the note) accuracy, known biases and testing for differential performance on demographic groups, and, for systems based on a large language model, 'the observed rate of hallucinations' and when they occur. UK268 expects buyers to seek vendor information on model architecture, training data, fine-tuning, known limitations and performance metrics, documentation of how bias was identified and addressed, and, for purchased systems, to verify performance with local data and test for bias. UK136 asks for evaluation questions about the algorithms, how the supplier selects variables and which techniques the model uses, and for known data limitations to be put in the invitation to tender with suppliers asked how they will address them; UK174 asks drafters to understand the supplier's AI approach. UK139, addressed to regulators, says they could encourage supply-chain actors to share testing and due-diligence information for others' procurement decisions. Strength ranges from 'consider asking' (UK099) to 'should' (UK268), and only UK268 goes beyond collecting the supplier's account to testing the system on the buyer's own data.
themes.holders: The buyer ('you (as buyer of an AI system)', 'The organisation', central government procurement teams); suppliers, vendors and developers as information providers; regulators and 'actors in the AI supply chain' (UK139).
themes.binding: Good practice and recommendations ('consider asking', 'should', imperative); UK139 non-binding ('could also encourage'). No consequence stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: before contract or purchase (tender evaluation and due diligence). Compared against: the supplier's own reported figures; UK268 adds verification against the buyer's local data; UK099 compares performance across demographic groups. Metric or threshold: accuracy, hallucination rate and the conditions in which hallucinations occur, differential performance, fairness metrics and performance metrics are named; no threshold is set. Who: the buyer asks and the supplier reports; who carries out UK268's verification and bias testing is not stated. What happens with the result: not stated (use in bid evaluation [inference] for UK136's evaluation questions).

themes.theme: Information flowing from suppliers and developers during use
themes.definition: Continuing flows of information from suppliers and developers to the deploying body once a system is in use, for monitoring, explaining outputs and giving notice of change.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK268 expects an organisation that lacks details of a third-party system's data to receive regular data quality reports from the third party, and UK099 says the body's own fairness monitoring should include information from suppliers. UK136 asks the buyer to establish with the supplier how the model's efficacy will be monitored once deployed, and notes that an AI system's functionality and consequences often become evident only in deployment, requiring extended communication between buyer and supplier. UK010 (Ofgem) says the supply chain has a role in explaining AI outputs to users at a level proportionate to risk, and UK139 says regulators could encourage developers to give deployers transparency and explainability information and to enable informed safety assessments. UK190 is the only binding instance: under DWP policy, suppliers 'must' inform DWP where AI will be incorporated into existing services or software. Most passages leave unstated who monitors, how often and against what standard.
themes.holders: Providers: third parties, suppliers, 'The supply chain', AI developers; recipients: the organisation or buyer; regulators as encouragers (UK139); 'Suppliers and their third parties' (UK190).
themes.binding: Mandatory by departmental policy in UK190; elsewhere 'should', recommended, 'has an important role to play' or 'could be encouraged'. No consequence stated; UK136 names a risk ('An inaccurate model can result in erroneous decisions that negatively impact citizens', truncated in the input).
themes.checks: Post-deployment monitoring involving suppliers: trigger: ongoing once deployed ('regular' data quality reports in UK268; 'once deployed' in UK136); compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: model efficacy (UK136), data quality (UK268) and fairness (UK099) are named, no threshold; who: left to agreement between buyer and supplier (UK136), the third party reports and the organisation receives (UK268); what happens with the result: not stated.

themes.theme: Securing supplier information for the public transparency record (ATRS)
themes.definition: Steps for obtaining from suppliers the information a public body needs to complete an Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard record, and for limiting what is withheld on commercial grounds.
themes.what_is_set_out: The ATRS guidance (UK086) encourages organisations to ask their commercial contact for details the supplier holds, explaining why algorithmic transparency matters, and to highlight it if the tool is in mandatory scope; it says issues over what to publish can usually be managed by consulting teams and relevant third-party suppliers during drafting. UK085 says public bodies procuring from vendors should make the expected level of transparency clear in the invitation to tender, and encourages them to work with their supply chains from the start to minimise information withheld for commercial reasons. UK174 says contracts 'can be drafted' to require supplier transparency on the ATRS information categories, and UK099 calls it 'helpful' to ensure suppliers provide all the ATRS information. None of these passages places a duty on the supplier itself (the coder notes say so for UK086), so the leverage is the buyer's tender and contract [inference].
themes.holders: Organisations completing ATRS records ('you'); 'Public bodies that are procuring solutions from vendors'; 'Public authorities'; 'the public sector (contracting bodies); third-party suppliers' (UK174); suppliers as counterparties.
themes.binding: Encouraged, 'should', 'can be drafted', 'it's helpful'. No consequence stated.

themes.definition: Arrangements governing what data passes between the public body and suppliers or other parties, on what terms and where it is processed.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 notes that data controllers may need additional safeguards, such as international data transfer agreements, where personal data is processed in jurisdictions whose data protection regime is not deemed adequate. UK099 asks teams to share data through a robust, privacy-preserving governance regime with safeguards (per the note) for security, lawful basis and retention. UK136 asks buyers to define whether and how data will be shared with vendors during procurement and the project, to give the same data to all suppliers at the same time in line with data protection law, and to consider non-disclosure agreements. AI_Insights says that where data sovereignty is a concern the user organisation 'must' clarify the vendor's data processing profile, including geolocation, ownership and usage. The concern throughout is control of the public body's data, not the tool's outputs.
themes.holders: 'Data controllers' (UK174); 'your team' (UK099); central government departments procuring AI and vendors (UK136); 'you (user organisation); the vendor' (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: Statutory where data protection law is restated (international transfers; 'acting in accordance with Data Protection legislation and GDPR'); 'must' in AI_Insights guidance with binding force not stated; otherwise recommended. No consequence stated beyond UK174's remark that processing outside the UK increases risk.
